nonlinear-001.question: The polarization P of a material is written as a power series in the electric field E: P = ε₀(χ⁽¹⁾E + χ⁽²⁾E² + χ⁽³⁾E³ + …). Why are nonlinear optical effects such as second-harmonic generation hardly observed with light from lamps, becoming prominent only with the intense light of focused pulsed lasers?
choices: Because nonlinear effects can in principle occur only with coherent light whose phases are aligned
Because χ⁽²⁾ and χ⁽³⁾ are extremely small, so the E² and E³ terms become non-negligible relative to the linear term only when the optical field is very strong
Because higher-order polarization arises only when the photon energy exceeds the band gap
nonlinear-001.explanation: The ratio of the higher-order terms to the linear term is roughly (optical field)/(the internal field of an atom, about 5×10¹¹ V/m), which is tiny for the field of ordinary light. In a focused pulsed laser, the optical field reaches around 10⁸ V/m (an intensity of about 1 GW/cm²), and the E² and E³ terms become large enough to observe. Nonlinear effects are set by field strength and occur even with incoherent light if it is intense enough (lasers simply have the advantage in phase matching and focusability). Also, wavelength conversion is normally done in a transparent, non-absorbing wavelength range; the photon energy need not exceed the band gap, and absorption actually makes the crystal more prone to damage.

nonlinear-002.question: Light from a 1064 nm Nd:YAG laser is passed through a nonlinear optical crystal to generate the second harmonic. Which correctly gives the wavelength of the resulting light and the relationship between photons?
choices: 532 nm; two fundamental photons produce one photon
2128 nm; one fundamental photon splits into two photons
About 752 nm (1064 nm divided by √2); the frequency rises by √2 because the intensity is squared
nonlinear-002.explanation: In second-harmonic generation (SHG), two photons at frequency ω disappear and one photon at 2ω is created. From energy conservation, ħω + ħω = ħ(2ω), the frequency doubles and the wavelength halves to 1064/2 = 532 nm, green light. 2128 nm is the wavelength of the reverse process in which a photon splits in two (degenerate optical parametric generation). The SH intensity being proportional to the square of the fundamental intensity is a separate matter from frequency: the frequency is exactly doubled, not multiplied by √2. A nonlinear crystal does not absorb and re-emit light; it stays transparent and mediates the exchange of energy between light waves.

nonlinear-003.question: In bulk silica glass and optical fiber, second-harmonic generation hardly occurs even with intense light. What is the main reason?
choices: Because glass also has zero third-order susceptibility χ⁽³⁾, so no nonlinear effects occur at all
Because glass strongly absorbs 532 nm green light, so the generated second harmonic is lost immediately
Because glass is an isotropic material with inversion symmetry, so its second-order susceptibility χ⁽²⁾ is zero
nonlinear-003.explanation: In a material with inversion symmetry, reversing the field must reverse the polarization, but the E² term does not change sign, so χ⁽²⁾ = 0. Amorphous materials such as glass and centrosymmetric crystals such as silicon fall into this category, so SHG and the Pockels effect use crystals that lack inversion symmetry, such as LiNbO₃, KTP and BBO. χ⁽³⁾, on the other hand, is nonzero in every material, and in fiber the Kerr effect, self-phase modulation and four-wave mixing are real problems, so the option claiming that χ⁽³⁾ is also zero is wrong. Silica glass is nearly transparent even at 532 nm, so absorption is not the reason.

nonlinear-004.question: The second harmonic is generated in a phase-matched nonlinear crystal. In the range where conversion efficiency is low and the fundamental is barely depleted (the undepleted-pump approximation), by what factor does the second-harmonic power change when the fundamental power is doubled? (The beam shape and crystal are unchanged.)
choices: 2 times
4 times
8 times
nonlinear-004.explanation: The second harmonic is radiated by the nonlinear polarization P(2ω) ∝ χ⁽²⁾E(ω)², so the SH field is proportional to the square of the fundamental field, and the SH power to the square of the fundamental power (P₂ω ∝ d²L²P_ω²/A, where A is the beam area). Doubling the fundamental increases the SH by 2² = 4 times, and the conversion efficiency P₂ω/P_ω also doubles. 2 times assumes a linear response, and 8 times confuses this with third-harmonic generation by χ⁽³⁾, which scales as the cube. This square-law dependence is why, at the same average power, pulses with high peak power or tightly focused beams convert more efficiently. At high efficiency, the fundamental is depleted and the relationship departs from the square law.

nonlinear-005.question: In second-harmonic generation, crystal dispersion makes the refractive indices of the fundamental and second harmonic differ, so the process is not phase-matched (Δk ≠ 0). How does the second-harmonic intensity behave as the crystal length L is increased?
choices: It keeps increasing in proportion to L²
It keeps increasing in proportion to L, but more slowly than when phase-matched
It peaks at the coherence length Lc = π/Δk, then decreases, rising and falling repeatedly, so making the crystal longer than Lc does not make it stronger
nonlinear-005.explanation: With a phase mismatch Δk = k₂ω − 2kω, the second harmonic generated at each point in the crystal gradually slips in phase. The SH intensity is proportional to sin²(ΔkL/2)/(Δk/2)²: it peaks at L = π/Δk (the coherence length Lc), then decreases as the out-of-phase contribution generated beyond that point cancels it, returning to zero at 2Lc. It thus oscillates, with its maximum limited to (2/Δk)². Continuing growth in proportion to L² happens only with phase matching, Δk = 0, and growth in proportion to L does not hold either. Lc is usually short, from a few to a few tens of micrometers, so phase matching is essential for efficient conversion.

nonlinear-006.question: The second harmonic (0.775 µm) of 1.55 µm light is generated by quasi-phase matching in periodically poled lithium niobate (PPLN). Taking the index difference n(0.775 µm) − n(1.55 µm) = 0.0375 and the coherence length Lc = λω/(4Δn) (λω is the fundamental wavelength), which value is closest to the poling period Λ needed for first-order quasi-phase matching?
choices: About 20.7 µm
About 10.3 µm
About 41.3 µm
nonlinear-006.explanation: The coherence length is Lc = 1.55/(4 × 0.0375) ≈ 10.3 µm. In quasi-phase matching, the polarization (the sign of χ⁽²⁾) is reversed every Lc, just as the SH would start to decrease, canceling the phase slip so the intensity keeps growing. One period contains one up and one down domain, so it is 2Lc: Λ = 2Lc = λω/(2Δn) ≈ 20.7 µm. About 10.3 µm takes Lc itself as the period, and about 41.3 µm uses the wrong factor, λω/Δn. Quasi-phase matching lets all the interacting waves share the same polarization, so the largest nonlinear coefficient, d₃₃, can be used, and there is no walk-off, so it is widely used for wavelength conversion. Changing the period lets the phase-matched wavelength be designed.

nonlinear-007.question: The second harmonic is generated in BBO, a negative uniaxial crystal (ne < no), by type I birefringent phase matching. Which correctly describes the choice of polarizations and propagation direction?
choices: Make both the fundamental and the second harmonic ordinary rays, and send the light along the crystal's optic axis
Make the fundamental an ordinary ray and the second harmonic an extraordinary ray, choosing the angle θ from the optic axis so that no(ω) = ne(2ω, θ)
Make the fundamental an extraordinary ray and the second harmonic an ordinary ray, and send the light perpendicular to the optic axis
nonlinear-007.explanation: In a normally dispersive material, the index is larger at shorter wavelengths, so with the same polarization n(2ω) > n(ω) and phase matching is impossible. In a negative uniaxial crystal, the extraordinary index is smaller than the ordinary index, and ne(2ω, θ) varies from no(2ω) to ne(2ω) with the angle θ between the propagation direction and the optic axis. Type I phase matching (o + o → e) makes the fundamental ordinary and the SH extraordinary and tunes to the angle where ne(2ω, θ) = no(ω). Making both ordinary leaves the dispersion uncompensated, and along the optic axis birefringence has no effect. Making the fundamental extraordinary cannot satisfy the condition in a negative crystal, because ne(ω) < no(2ω).

nonlinear-008.question: The fundamental of an Nd:YAG laser (1064 nm) and its second harmonic (532 nm) are mixed by sum-frequency generation in a nonlinear crystal to make the third harmonic. Which value is closest to the resulting wavelength?
choices: About 798 nm
About 1596 nm
About 355 nm
nonlinear-008.explanation: Sum-frequency generation adds frequencies, ω₃ = ω₁ + ω₂, which in wavelength is 1/λ₃ = 1/λ₁ + 1/λ₂. 1/λ₃ = 1/1064 + 1/532 = 3/1064, so λ₃ = 1064/3 ≈ 354.7 nm, ultraviolet light at about 355 nm. This is exactly three times the fundamental frequency — the third harmonic used for ultraviolet laser machining and other applications. About 798 nm averages the two wavelengths, and about 1596 nm adds the wavelengths directly (1064 + 532), the classic mistake of adding wavelengths instead of frequencies. Two stages of SHG and sum-frequency generation in χ⁽²⁾ crystals produce the third harmonic more efficiently than direct tripling through χ⁽³⁾.

nonlinear-009.question: An optical parametric oscillator (OPO) pumped at 532 nm produces signal light at 800 nm. Which value is closest to the wavelength of the idler generated at the same time?
choices: About 1588 nm
About 320 nm
About 268 nm
nonlinear-009.explanation: In an optical parametric process, one pump photon splits into two photons, the signal and the idler, with energy conservation ωp = ωs + ωi. In wavelength, 1/λi = 1/λp − 1/λs = 1/532 − 1/800, so λi ≈ 1588 nm. About 320 nm adds the frequencies, 1/532 + 1/800, giving the sum-frequency wavelength — the reverse of the photon-splitting OPO. About 268 nm subtracts the wavelengths (800 − 532). Both signal and idler are longer in wavelength than the pump, and changing the phase-matching conditions (crystal angle, temperature, poling period) shifts the split between them while conserving energy, so the wavelength can be tuned continuously.

nonlinear-010.question: Which correctly describes an optical parametric oscillator (OPO)?
choices: It creates a population inversion in a gain medium and amplifies by stimulated emission, so the oscillation wavelength is set by the medium's energy levels
Its main use is generating light at shorter wavelengths than the pump
Gain arises from an instantaneous process that stores no energy in the medium, and the output wavelength can be tuned over a wide range by changing the phase-matching conditions
nonlinear-010.explanation: The gain of an OPO is optical parametric amplification through χ⁽²⁾, in which energy flows directly from the pump to the signal and idler. No excitation is stored in atomic or molecular levels, so no population inversion is needed, and gain exists only while the pump is present. The output wavelength is set not by particular levels but by energy conservation and phase matching, so changing the crystal angle, temperature or PPLN poling period tunes it widely, from the visible to the mid-infrared. In this respect its mechanism differs from a laser, whose wavelength is set by energy levels. By energy conservation, the signal and idler are always longer in wavelength than the pump; shorter wavelengths come from second-harmonic or sum-frequency generation.

nonlinear-011.question: Take the nonlinear refractive index of silica glass as n₂ = 2.6×10⁻²⁰ m²/W. Which value is closest to the refractive index change from the optical Kerr effect, Δn = n₂I, for light with an intensity of 1 GW/cm²?
choices: About 2.6×10⁻¹¹
About 2.6×10⁻⁷
About 2.6×10⁻¹⁵
nonlinear-011.explanation: The key is consistent units. 1 GW/cm² = 10⁹ W / 10⁻⁴ m² = 10¹³ W/m², so Δn = n₂I = 2.6×10⁻²⁰ × 10¹³ = 2.6×10⁻⁷. About 2.6×10⁻¹¹ multiplies by the number 10⁹ with the intensity still in W/cm², and about 2.6×10⁻¹⁵ applies the conversion 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m² backwards, taking the intensity as 10⁵ W/m². Δn looks very small, but over 1 m at 1.55 µm the phase change 2πΔnL/λ reaches about 1 rad. Over long distances, as in fiber, or in self-focusing, where the index rises toward the beam center so the beam acts as a lens, this small change has large effects.

nonlinear-012.question: Among electro-optic effects, in which an applied electric field changes the refractive index, which correctly describes the difference between the Pockels effect and the Kerr effect?
choices: In the Pockels effect the index change is proportional to the field and occurs only in crystals lacking inversion symmetry; in the Kerr effect it is proportional to the square of the field and occurs in any material
In the Pockels effect the index change is proportional to the square of the field; in the Kerr effect it is proportional to the field
Both arise from χ⁽³⁾, and the only difference is whether the applied field is DC or the optical field
nonlinear-012.explanation: The Pockels effect (linear electro-optic effect) comes from χ⁽²⁾, and the index change is proportional to the applied field E. Because it needs χ⁽²⁾, it occurs only in crystals lacking inversion symmetry such as LiNbO₃, and reversing the field reverses the sign of the index change. LN modulators for optical communications and electro-optic Q-switches use it. The Kerr effect (quadratic electro-optic effect) comes from χ⁽³⁾, with Δn ∝ E², and occurs in every material, including glasses and liquids. When it is driven by the light's own field it is the optical Kerr effect, with Δn = n₂I, proportional to intensity. The option that gives the Pockels effect the E² dependence reverses the proportionalities, and the option attributing both effects to χ⁽³⁾ is wrong because the Pockels effect comes from χ⁽²⁾, not χ⁽³⁾.

nonlinear-013.question: Light with a peak power of 100 mW is launched into a single-mode fiber with a nonlinear coefficient γ = 1.3 /(W·km). If the fiber's effective length is 20 km, which value is closest to the maximum nonlinear phase shift from self-phase modulation, φNL = γPLeff?
choices: About 0.13 rad
About 2600 rad
About 2.6 rad
nonlinear-013.explanation: φNL = γPLeff = 1.3 W⁻¹km⁻¹ × 0.1 W × 20 km = 2.6 rad. Multiplying by 100 without converting the power to watts gives about 2600 rad, and forgetting the effective length gives the per-kilometer value, about 0.13 rad. φNL is largest at the center of the pulse, where intensity peaks; because the phase follows the time variation of intensity, the instantaneous frequency shifts and the spectrum broadens. Broadening becomes noticeable once φNL exceeds about 1 rad, and for a Gaussian pulse at around 1.5π the center of the spectrum dips and splits into two peaks. In WDM transmission, this phase change combines with dispersion to degrade waveforms, which caps the power per channel.

nonlinear-014.question: When an intense unchirped optical pulse travels through a short fiber in which dispersion is negligible, what change does self-phase modulation (n₂ > 0) cause?
choices: The pulse's temporal waveform is compressed and shortened, and the spectral width is unchanged
The temporal waveform is unchanged, but a frequency chirp arises that shifts the leading half of the pulse to longer wavelengths and the trailing half to shorter wavelengths, broadening the spectrum
The leading half shifts to shorter wavelengths and the trailing half to longer wavelengths, and the spectrum narrows
nonlinear-014.explanation: In self-phase modulation, the refractive index follows the time variation of intensity, n = n₀ + n₂I(t), so the phase becomes φNL(t) ∝ I(t). The instantaneous frequency shift is δω = −dφNL/dt, so the frequency drops (longer wavelengths) on the leading half of the pulse, where intensity rises, and rises (shorter wavelengths) on the trailing half, where it falls. New frequency components appear and the spectrum broadens, but only the phase changes, so without dispersion the temporal intensity waveform stays the same. The waveform changes only when this chirp combines with dispersion. The option shifting the leading half to shorter wavelengths reverses the direction, and the spectrum does not narrow for an unchirped input pulse.

nonlinear-015.question: Which correctly describes the condition for an optical soliton (fundamental soliton), which travels through an optical fiber while keeping its pulse shape?
choices: The chirp from self-phase modulation balances anomalous dispersion (D > 0), in which shorter-wavelength components travel faster
The chirp from self-phase modulation balances normal dispersion (D < 0), in which longer-wavelength components travel faster
The fiber loss balances the gain from self-phase modulation
nonlinear-015.explanation: Self-phase modulation shifts the leading half of the pulse to longer wavelengths and the trailing half to shorter wavelengths. In the anomalous-dispersion regime (β₂ < 0, D > 0), shorter-wavelength components have higher group velocity, so the short-wavelength components at the back move forward and the long-wavelength components at the front fall back, and dispersive broadening and the SPM chirp cancel. When peak power and pulse width balance exactly (N = 1), the pulse becomes a fundamental soliton that keeps its shape. In standard single-mode fiber, the 1.55 µm band is in the anomalous-dispersion regime. With normal dispersion, the long-wavelength components move further ahead, so the pulse only spreads. SPM changes only phase and produces no gain, and loss makes a soliton gradually break up, so the option balancing fiber loss against gain from SPM is also wrong.
